strengths: WildFeedback addresses a relevant NLP problem: converting naturally occurring feedback in multi-turn conversations into preference-training data. Explicit preference summaries provide a useful connection between user feedback, response generation, and evaluation.

The GPT-4-generated dataset produces substantial improvements across three model families. Table 3 reports AlpacaEval 2 length-controlled gains of 10.6–14.3 percentage points, alongside Arena-Hard improvements. These results support the dataset’s utility for improving automated instruction-following performance.

The feedback detector receives an initial human validation involving four experts and 50 conversations. Reporting precision, recall, and inter-annotator agreement provides useful evidence about extraction quality; DSAT precision reaches 83.3%.

The pipeline is understandable, and the appendices provide detailed rubrics, extraction and evaluation prompts, model identifiers, and principal training hyperparameters. The reported separation of users and conversations between training and evaluation is an appropriate safeguard.
weaknesses: The central claim of closer alignment with actual users lacks independent validation. GPT-4o summarizes preferences, generates expert targets, filters on-policy pairs, and judges responses using those summaries. Figure 2 demonstrates that checklists change the judge’s choices, without establishing that the changed choices better match users’ judgments. The human study validates only SAT/DSAT detection, not summary fidelity, generated preference pairs, or final response rankings. Human evaluation grounded in the original feedback is needed to substantiate the claimed improvement over synthetic-feedback biases.

The experiments do not isolate the contribution of user feedback. Additional SFT plus DPO is compared only with off-the-shelf models. Missing controls include training on the same prompts with GPT-4 responses generated without extracted preferences, a comparable existing preference dataset, and SFT alone. Furthermore, expert and on-policy datasets differ in size, filtering, and rejected-response source. Consequently, the observed gains cannot establish how much benefit comes specifically from the proposed feedback mechanism.

The evaluation’s representativeness is unsubstantiated. Section 4 deliberately selects centrally shared preferences within 70 clusters and tasks similar to training. Even for the stated objective of learning broadly shared preferences, embedding similarity and equal per-cluster sampling do not establish population-majority preferences. DSAT recall of 48.4% further raises coverage questions. An uncurated evaluation with separate users, together with feedback-category and distribution analyses, would strengthen the generalization claims.

The claim that training does not compromise other benchmarks contradicts Table 3. On-policy Mistral declines from 17.1 to 12.9 on AlpacaEval 2 LC, 12.6 to 10.3 on Arena-Hard, and 6.71 to 6.42 on MT-Bench. It also loses more often than it wins under checklist-free WildFeedback evaluation. Conclusions should distinguish the two dataset variants. Uncertainty estimates are also absent despite repeated claims of significant improvement, including small MT-Bench changes.

Reproducibility is incomplete despite the useful appendix. The manuscript promises future dataset availability but supplies no dataset or code link. It also leaves unspecified the embeddings and precise similarity procedure used for evaluation curation, split manifests, data-generation decoding settings, and hyperparameter-selection protocol. These details are material because the generated dataset and curated evaluation underpin the contribution. Together with the missing validation and controls, these gaps prevent a positive Findings recommendation at present.
